extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists and educated public, late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Mixed-content scientific journal issue containing editorial policies, letters, methodological notes, book-review standards, and commentary on professional training; the extracted rubrics cover publication policies and recommended experimental/monographic practices found in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval education — encourage specialities and selective training
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to speak of the navy as a scientific profession...few have the time, even if they had the disposition, to go deep into scientific study...That beyond the regular line of the service there are duties which call for a higher and more extended knowledge, is freely admitted by all; and we are convinced that these duties will be more efficiently performed by officers specially educated for them, than by others nominated indiscriminately or by roster...We conceive that it is by allowing, nay, encouraging these specialities to develop themselves to the utmost, that the greatest perfection in the aggregate is to be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force practically-minded officers through distasteful high mathematics or foreign languages; form a Naval Staff and encourage special training (example given: gunnery certificates already held by about one-sixth of lieutenants). Select specialists by interest/taste from the whole service rather than by birth or roster; provide encouragement and hope of reward to sustain study amid active service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to the Editor — handling and acceptance policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish anonymous letters; statements by correspondents are their own responsibility and not endorsed by the Editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarimetric observation method for the solar corona
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a Savart’s polariscope attached to a telescope, converted into a polarimeter by passing light through four plates of crown glass mounted in a frame movable on an axis at right angles to the direction of the bands; instrument fixed in front of the eye-piece of an equatorially-mounted telescope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align bands radial to the Sun (so bands are horizontal or appropriate orientation); turning the glass plates produces known polarisation, and the angle required to extinguish bands gives a measure of the polarisation (differential polarimeter). Ensure the plane of polarisation coincides with the direction of the bands to measure; use measurements at different distances from the limb to detect variation (example result: corona radially polarised and polarisation increases with distance from limb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical verification and errata practice in experimental appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: On discovering numerical errors in an illustrative appendix to an acoustical experiments paper: 'some strange numerical errors, which perhaps it will be well to point out, lest some of your readers should make use of the numbers given at the end of the paper without previously testing them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and readers should verify arithmetic in numerical appendices before using published numbers; publish errata with corrected calculations and explicit substituted passages when errors are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for measuring linear expansion via a 'thermometer of translation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal: place a highly expansible body with a fine needle point (or clamping screws) on a sloping serrated frame; when the body expands its upper end advances up the frame; repeat expansions and contractions so cumulative translation becomes measurable; final single reading suffices for the whole series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To double readings for expansion use clamping screws on upright rods instead of a needle point; place the bar on rollers within a vessel of water/steam at different temperatures; tighten/loosen screws appropriately before expansion/contraction; repeat heating/cooling many times to accumulate measurable translation; divide total translation by number of repeats, degrees of temperature change, and original length to compute coefficient of linear expansion. This cumulative-repetition approach is recommended for minute expansions as more reliable than some classical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for acceptable theories of the origin of insects
rubrics_metrics.description: Any theory of the origin of insects ought to account for, or at least show the origin of, those most characteristic organs of the class, the wings. The origin of insect metamorphoses remains a major difficulty which a satisfactory theory must address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing evolutionary scenarios for insect origins, explicitly explain the origin of wings and account for metamorphosis (i.e., whether perfect forms derived from larval forms or vice versa); avoid neglecting the most characteristic class organs in explanatory hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for taxonomic monographs (Laube's Echinoderm monograph example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laube 'carefully describes fourteen new or previously unknown species...adds a new genus...The monograph contains a very valuable table showing the distribution of those species which occur elsewhere...it is accompanied by four quarto lithographic plates devoted to the local and new species, which are carefully figured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-quality taxonomic monograph should: describe new species in detail; justify and define any new genera; include distribution tables comparing occurrences across regions; provide carefully executed plates/figures of species. Emphasise clear figures and comparative distribution data to make the work a valuable contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for regional faunal catalogues (Hutton's Fishes of New Zealand example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangements and nomenclature adopted are those of Dr. Günther’s 'Catalogue of Fishes,' the most recent and by far the best authority on the subject...the twelve plates which accompany it, and which give the outline of about fifty of the most characteristic species, will be of great assistance to the unlearned colonist in his attempt to make out the correct names of the native fishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt up-to-date authoritative nomenclature (cite and follow the leading catalogue); include plates illustrating characteristic species to assist non-specialists and aid identification; prepare diagnoses and notes (e.g., on edibility) to increase practical usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reporting: description of instrument behaviour and crucial controls (illustrated by eclipse polarisation observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control experiments are crucial: e.g., placing bands at right angles to the plane of polarisation would yield black centred bands which would be increased by turning glass plates; measuring at locations about 90° from the vertex tests alternative hypotheses (e.g., reflection from Earth's unobserved portions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting observational phenomena, design crucial tests that distinguish competing hypotheses (orientation controls, selection of observation points, and instrument alignment). Report the expected instrument responses for each hypothesis and use those to support or refute explanatory accounts.
